## Last week, in one slide

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
An LLM is our neuron's training loop at scale: **tokens** become **vectors**; **attention** lets each token take what it needs from the others; the **block** is stacked dozens of times.

At the end, one **knob** per token — and **temperature** decides how boldly it picks.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
Pre-training, fine-tuning and RL are the same loop with different right answers.

It invents by design: there is always a top knob, even when the fact was never in the data.
:::
::::

## [Part 1]{.section-kicker} Look {.section-slide background-color="#AF1F25"}

## The question for the morning

### Is crypto risk predictable — and which part of it?

We will not answer it with a model. We answer it with four small questions, asked in order:

1. what is in the table?
2. how big are the moves?
3. how often does the "impossible" happen?
4. **does yesterday tell us anything about today?**

[Exploration is not "make charts". It is asking the data small questions until you know which question is worth a model.]{.explain}

## The table, and the worst day {.lab background-color="#2471a3"}

[LAB · session.ipynb § E1–E2]{.kicker}

::: {.callout-important title="Bet"}
SPY has empty days, Bitcoin has none. Out of every seven days, how many is SPY missing?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Bet"}
Bitcoin's worst single day since 2018: how much did it lose, and when?
:::

## Two questions that sound alike

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Direction
Bitcoin went **up** today.

Is it more likely to go up tomorrow?
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Size
Bitcoin moved **a lot** today, either way.

Is it more likely to move a lot tomorrow?
:::
::::

::: {.callout-important title="Bet"}
Which one has memory — direction, size, both, neither?
:::

## The answer

![](img/w03-memory.svg){fig-align="center" width="86%"}

[The **autocorrelation** compares a series with itself, *k* days earlier.]{.explain}

## Calm follows calm. Storms follow storms. {.statement}

[It is called **volatility clustering**, and we found it before training anything. It already tells us which question a model can help with — and which one it cannot.]{.muted}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Will Bitcoin be up next week?**

`y_dir`
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Will next week be more volatile than usual?**

`y_vol` — "usual" is the median of the past year
:::
::::

## Before the model: what does nothing score?

::: {.callout-important title="Bet"}
In what share of weeks did Bitcoin go up?
:::

. . .

**53%.** "Always say up" is right 53% of the time, with no data and no model.

[That is the **base rate**. And for volatility there is a smarter baseline anyone can write: **"next week will be like this week."** A model has to beat both.]{.explain}

## The black box: a random forest

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Hundreds of decision trees.** Each is a flowchart of yes/no questions on the features — *"is this week's volatility above 1.3 × usual?"* — grown on a slightly different sample of the past.

They **vote**. The share of votes is the probability.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
It finds curves and interactions on its own.

**What it cannot do is tell you whether it is right.**

That is the split's job — and ours.
:::
::::

[We open it in week 9. Today we judge it from the outside — which is what you will do with every vendor's model.]{.muted}

## Two splits {.lab background-color="#2471a3"}

[LAB · session.ipynb § M3]{.kicker}

Same features, same targets, same forest. Only the split changes.

1. **Honest:** learn on 2019–2023, judge on 2024 → today.
2. **The assistant's default:** `train_test_split` — shuffle the days, keep 30% aside.

::: {.callout-important title="Bet"}
Four numbers: AUC for direction and for volatility, honest and shuffled.
:::

[AUC: does the model rank the 1s above the 0s? 0.5 is a coin, 1.0 is perfect.]{.muted}

## Why the shuffled number lies {.clip background-color="#000000"}

<video class="clipvideo" width="1000" height="562" controls muted loop playsinline data-autoplay preload="auto" poster="media/w03_splits_poster.png"><source src="media/w03_splits.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video>

Shuffled, the model trains on Wednesday and Friday and is tested on Thursday. It is not predicting — it is remembering its neighbours.

## What came out

![](img/w03-results.svg){fig-align="center" width="88%"}

[Shuffled beats honest on both: that gap is leakage, not skill. Direction is a coin, as Part 1 said. Volatility is predictable — and the one-line rule beats the forest.]{.explain}

## Same data, same model. The question decides. {.statement}

[Whether ML has anything to offer depends on the question you ask it. Choosing the question is the manager's job — and looking first is how you choose.]{.muted}

## What did the black box look at?

![](img/w03-importance.svg){fig-align="center" width="88%"}

[A black box that agrees with what you saw by eye is one you can start to trust.]{.explain}

## Leak it on purpose {.lab background-color="#2471a3"}

[LAB · session.ipynb § your turn after M4]{.kicker}

The assistant offers to *"smooth"* the volatility: `rolling(7, center=True)`.

1. Add it as a feature. Keep the **honest** split.
2. Watch the AUC go from 0.60 to 0.69.
3. One sentence: why did the honest split not protect you?

[A leak looks exactly like success. This is the only safe place to learn what that feels like.]{.red}

## [Part 3]{.section-kicker} An LLM, called from code {.section-slide background-color="#AF1F25"}

## From tool to component

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Until now: a tool
You type into a chat. It answers. You copy.

Nothing is measured; every answer is a one-off.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### From today: a component
Your code calls it, with arguments **you** set:

- the **prompt** — what you ask
- the **system** message — who it is, what it may not do
- the **temperature** — last week's knob
- the **model**
:::
::::

[A component can be run 40 times, scored, compared with a rule — and priced. That is weeks 4 and 5, in miniature.]{.explain}

## The key is a password to a bank account {.statement}

[Never in a cell, a screenshot or a chat. In Colab it lives in 🔑 **Secrets**. Today I type mine into a hidden box: it stays in this runtime's memory and is gone when you close it.]{.muted}

[Forty dates is a small test: ±0.1 of AUC can be luck. And the bill — calls, tokens, dollars — is printed under the score. The rule costs nothing.]{.muted}
